questions.title: Skin macrophage of the epidermis
questions.question: The cells of the epidermis that act as skin macrophages are:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Keratinocytes are the epidermis's dominant, keratin-forming cell — they build the barrier, they do not patrol it for antigen.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Melanocytes are the epidermis's pigment-forming cell, supplying melanin to surrounding keratinocytes; they have no phagocytic or antigen-presenting role.
explanations.C: Correct. Langerhans cells are the epidermis's resident dendritic antigen-presenting cell, part of the mononuclear phagocyte system despite sitting among keratinocytes rather than in connective tissue. They arise from monocyte precursors like every other member of that system, take up antigen that penetrates the epidermis, and migrate to regional lymph nodes to present it to T cells, making them the skin's own local macrophage-lineage sentinel. This is the same distribution logic that places a monocyte-derived phagocyte under a different name in nearly every organ, Kupffer cells in the liver and microglia in the CNS among them.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Merkel cells are the epidermis's mechanoreceptor cell, associated with slowly adapting touch sensation, not phagocytosis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Basal cells are the proliferative stem-cell layer of the epidermis; their job is renewal, not immune surveillance.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the Langerhans cell as the epidermis's own member of the monocyte-derived mononuclear phagocyte system.

questions.title: Where the sebaceous gland duct opens
questions.question: Where does the duct of the sebaceous gland open?

options.B: The upper 1/3 of the hair follicle
options.C: The middle 1/3 of the hair follicle
options.D: The lower 1/3 of the hair follicle
options.E: The duct of the sweat gland

explanations.A: Incorrect. Reaching the skin surface directly is how an eccrine sweat gland duct behaves; the sebaceous gland's own short, wide duct empties into the hair follicle rather than opening independently onto the surface.
explanations.B: Correct. The sebaceous gland's short, wide excretory duct, lined by stratified squamous epithelium continuous with the follicle's outer root sheath, opens into the upper third of the hair follicle. This lets sebum coat the hair shaft as it emerges and spread onto the adjacent skin surface once the hair exits, keeping both hair and skin lubricated. The gland itself sits as an outgrowth from the follicle's external sheath, which is why its duct terminates back into that same follicle rather than forming an independent surface opening.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The middle third of the follicle is not where the sebaceous duct empties; the arrector pili muscle inserts near this general region of the follicle, not the gland's duct.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lower third of the follicle, near the bulb and matrix, is where the hair itself is generated, not where the sebaceous duct opens.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The sebaceous gland's duct is entirely separate from the sweat gland's duct; the two glandular systems do not share an outflow.

questions.learning_objective: State that the sebaceous gland's duct opens into the upper third of the hair follicle.

questions.title: The extra chromosome in Down syndrome
questions.question: Down syndrome has an extra chromosome number:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chromosome 9 is not the chromosome duplicated in Down syndrome; no named clinical syndrome in this teaching set is built on trisomy 9.
explanations.B: Correct. Down syndrome is trisomy 21 — the presence of three copies of chromosome 21 instead of the normal two, most often from nondisjunction during maternal meiosis I. It is the most common autosomal trisomy compatible with survival to birth, and the extra copy of this specific, gene-dense chromosome produces the syndrome's characteristic intellectual disability, dysmorphic facies and congenital heart defects. Chromosome 21 is deliberately chosen among exam distractors precisely because it is the smallest autosome, which is part of why trisomy 21 is survivable while trisomies of larger chromosomes generally are not.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Chromosome 4 is associated with a partial short-arm deletion (Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome), a structural loss, not an extra whole chromosome in Down syndrome.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chromosome 5 is associated with a partial short-arm deletion (cri-du-chat syndrome), not with Down syndrome's extra chromosome.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Chromosome 22 is not the trisomic chromosome in Down syndrome; it is deliberately placed near 21 among the options as a numerically close distractor.

questions.learning_objective: State that Down syndrome is trisomy 21, an extra copy of chromosome 21.

questions.title: Autosome count in human sperm
questions.question: How many autosomes are present in human sperm?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Eleven is half of 22, not the haploid autosome count; no meiotic product carries this number.
explanations.B: Correct. A human sperm is haploid, carrying 23 chromosomes in total — 22 autosomes plus a single sex chromosome (X or Y) — half of the diploid somatic formula of 44 autosomes plus one pair of sex chromosomes. This halving is exactly what meiosis achieves: each gamete receives one member of every homologous pair, so 22 autosomes rather than the 44 (22 pairs) present in a somatic cell. Fertilisation then restores the diploid 44+XX or 44+XY somatic formula by combining this sperm's 22+X/Y with the oocyte's own 22+X.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Forty-four autosomes is the diploid, somatic-cell count (22 pairs), not the haploid count carried by a single sperm.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Forty-five is neither the haploid nor the diploid autosome count; it does not correspond to a normal cell's chromosome complement.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Forty-six is the total chromosome number of a normal diploid somatic cell (44 autosomes plus 2 sex chromosomes), not the autosome count of a haploid gamete.

questions.learning_objective: State the haploid autosome count (22) carried by a human sperm, as half the diploid somatic formula.

questions.title: The longest stage of the cell cycle
questions.question: Which of the following represents the longest stage in the cell cycle?

explanations.A: Correct. Interphase — comprising G1, S and G2 — occupies the great majority of a dividing cell's cycle, commonly on the order of 90% or more of total cycle time, while the four mitotic stages together take up only a small remaining fraction. This is the period in which the cell grows, carries out its normal metabolic work, and replicates its DNA in S-phase, all before the comparatively brief, visually dramatic business of chromosome segregation in mitosis proper. A cell that appears "resting" under the microscope between divisions is, in fact, in this longest and most metabolically active stage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Prophase is one of the four short mitotic stages; even though it is typically the longest of the four mitotic stages themselves, it is still far shorter than interphase as a whole.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Metaphase, the brief alignment of chromosomes at the equatorial plate, is one of the shortest phases of the entire cycle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Anaphase, the rapid poleward separation of sister chromatids, is a brief mitotic stage, not the longest part of the cycle.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Telophase, reforming the nuclear envelope and completing division, is a short closing mitotic stage, not the cycle's longest phase.

questions.learning_objective: State that interphase, not any single mitotic stage, is the longest phase of the cell cycle.

questions.title: Interpreting a 47,XY+21 karyotype
questions.question: If chromosomal karyotyping was performed and resulted in a 47, XY+21 karyotype, what is the possible diagnosis of the case?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Edward syndrome is trisomy 18, karyotype 47,XY+18 or 47,XX+18, not +21.
explanations.B: Correct. The notation 47,XY+21 reads as 47 total chromosomes, a male sex-chromosome constitution (XY), and one extra copy of chromosome 21 — exactly the karyotype of Down syndrome (trisomy 21). Reading a karyotype string this way — total count, sex chromosomes, then any named extra or missing chromosome after the plus or minus sign — is the standard notation used across every trisomy and monosomy syndrome. Here the "+21" is unambiguous: three copies of chromosome 21 rather than two is the chromosomal basis of Down syndrome regardless of the patient's sex chromosomes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cri-du-chat syndrome is a partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (46,XY or XX,5p-), a structural loss on a normal chromosome count, not an extra chromosome 21.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Wolf (Wolf-Hirschhorn) syndrome is a partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 4, again a structural deletion, not an extra chromosome 21.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A "YY syndrome" (47,XYY) is an extra Y sex chromosome, not an extra autosome 21, and would be written 47,XYY rather than 47,XY+21.

questions.learning_objective: Read a 47,XY+21 karyotype notation as Down syndrome (trisomy 21).

questions.title: Commonest mechanism behind Down syndrome
questions.question: Which of the following represents the commonest mechanism of genetic abnormality in Down syndrome?

explanations.A: Correct. The great majority of Down syndrome cases arise from nondisjunction — failure of the paired chromosome 21 homologues to separate — during the first meiotic division of the primary oocyte, i.e. in the maternal gamete. Because a human primary oocyte remains arrested in meiosis I from fetal life until the cycle in which it is finally ovulated (sometimes for decades), this arrested state is thought to make maternal meiosis I especially prone to nondisjunction, which is also why the risk of trisomy 21 rises sharply with advancing maternal age. Paternal nondisjunction, translocation and mosaicism all also cause Down syndrome, but each accounts for only a small minority of cases compared with this maternal meiosis I mechanism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Nondisjunction can occur in the paternal gamete too, but it is a much less common source of trisomy 21 than maternal meiosis I nondisjunction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 14 (and chromosome 21) causes a minority of Down syndrome cases, notably the familial, inherited form, but it is not the commonest mechanism overall.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Translocation to any autosome describes the translocation mechanism broadly, but translocation as a whole is still a minority cause next to maternal nondisjunction.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Mosaic Down syndrome, in which only some of the body's cells carry the extra chromosome 21 from a post-fertilisation mitotic error, is the rarest of the recognised mechanisms.

questions.learning_objective: State that maternal meiosis I nondisjunction is the commonest mechanism producing Down syndrome.

questions.title: Highest DNA-to-cytoplasm ratio in the mitotic cycle
questions.question: At which stage of the mitotic cell cycle is there the highest ratio of DNA to cytoplasm?

explanations.A: Incorrect. At the beginning of G1 the cell has just completed mitosis and cytokinesis, so it holds an unreplicated (single, 46-s) DNA content in a full-sized cytoplasm — the lowest, not the highest, DNA-to-cytoplasm ratio of the cycle.
explanations.B: Correct. S-phase replicates the cell's entire DNA content, doubling it from 46-s to 46-d chromosomes, while the cytoplasm itself has not yet had the chance to grow further or divide. The instant S-phase completes is therefore the point at which the cell holds its full doubled DNA content within the smallest cytoplasmic volume it will have for the rest of the cycle, before G2's further growth or mitosis's eventual division dilutes that ratio again. G2 and mitosis keep the same doubled DNA content, but the cell's cytoplasmic volume only increases from this point onward until division halves it, so the ratio is highest right at the S-to-G2 transition.
explanations.C: Incorrect. By the end of G2 the DNA content is still doubled (46-d) as it was at the end of S-phase, but the cytoplasm has continued to grow through G2, so the ratio has fallen slightly from its S-phase peak.
explanations.D: Incorrect. By the end of telophase the cell has completed cytokinesis and division, restoring the single (46-s) DNA content in each daughter cell — a low ratio, not the cycle's highest.
explanations.E: Incorrect. At the beginning of metaphase the DNA content is still doubled, but cytoplasmic growth through G2 has already diluted the ratio below its S-phase peak.

questions.learning_objective: State that the DNA-to-cytoplasm ratio peaks at the end of S-phase, once DNA content has doubled but cytoplasmic growth has not yet caught up.

questions.title: Naming the process that exchanges chromosome material
questions.question: Which of the following represents the process by which maternal and paternal chromosomes exchange their material?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Synapsis is the pairing of homologous maternal and paternal chromosomes at zygotene; it brings the chromosomes together but is not itself the exchange of material between them.
explanations.B: Correct. Crossing over is the reciprocal exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of paired homologous (one maternal, one paternal) chromosomes, occurring at pachytene of meiotic prophase I once synapsis has aligned the homologues. It is the mechanism absent from mitosis but present in meiosis, and it is exactly what shuffles maternal and paternal genetic material into new combinations on each chromatid, which is the source of genetic recombination and variation among gametes. Crossing over depends on synapsis having already paired the homologues, since an exchange between two DNA strands can only happen once they are physically aligned.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Interphase is the period of growth and DNA replication before division begins; it precedes meiosis's pairing and exchange events rather than being the exchange itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Dyad formation describes the paired sister-chromatid structure of a replicated chromosome, not the process of exchanging material between maternal and paternal homologues.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cytokinesis is the physical division of the cytoplasm into two daughter cells at the end of a division cycle, unrelated to chromosomal material exchange.

questions.learning_objective: Name crossing over as the process that exchanges genetic material between paired maternal and paternal chromosomes.

questions.title: How many DNA replications meiosis involves
questions.question: Meiosis involves one cycle of:

options.C: Arrangement of chromosomes in cell equator

explanations.A: Correct. Meiosis has only one round of DNA replication (one S-phase), which occurs before the first meiotic division, but that single replicated DNA content is then distributed across two successive divisions with no intervening S-phase between them. The first division separates homologous chromosomes and the second, mitosis-like division separates sister chromatids, so one replication event ultimately yields four haploid cells rather than the two diploid cells a single mitotic division would give. Condensation, spindle formation, equatorial alignment, chromosome separation and cytokinesis, by contrast, all happen twice in meiosis, once in each division.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chromosomal condensation and spindle formation occur in both meiotic divisions, not once — they happen again in the second division, which repeats much of the first division's mechanics.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Equatorial alignment of chromosomes occurs at metaphase of both meiotic divisions, not just once.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chromosome separation occurs in both divisions — homologues separate in the first, sister chromatids in the second — so it is not a single, one-cycle event either.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cytokinesis follows both meiotic divisions, producing first two cells and then four, so it too happens twice, not once.

questions.learning_objective: State that meiosis has a single round of DNA replication feeding two successive divisions.

questions.title: Recognising pyknosis
questions.question: Which of the following changes describes pyknosis?

options.A: The nucleus dissolves and finally disappears
options.B: The nucleus is broken into small fragments
options.D: The nucleus becomes smaller, darker and eccentric
options.E: The nucleus becomes larger and highly vesicular

explanations.A: Incorrect. A nucleus dissolving and disappearing describes karyolysis, the fading of nuclear basophilia, a different one of the three classic necrotic nuclear changes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A nucleus breaking into small fragments describes karyorrhexis, which classically follows pyknosis rather than being pyknosis itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Highly condensed chromosomes describes the general appearance that underlies pyknosis, but the question asks for the change as it affects the whole nucleus, which "smaller, darker and eccentric" states more completely.
explanations.D: Correct. Pyknosis is shrinkage of the nucleus into a smaller, densely basophilic (darker-staining) mass, often displaced toward one side of the cell (eccentric), reflecting condensation of its chromatin into a solid, homogeneous clump. It is one of the three classic nuclear changes of necrosis, alongside karyorrhexis (fragmentation, which typically follows pyknosis) and karyolysis (fading and dissolution). Distinguishing pyknosis from karyorrhexis is a recurring exam point: pyknosis is shrinkage of the whole nucleus into a dense mass, while karyorrhexis is that mass breaking apart into fragments.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A larger, vesicular nucleus with pale, open chromatin describes an active, healthy nucleus, the opposite of the shrunken, dense pyknotic change.

questions.learning_objective: Describe pyknosis as nuclear shrinkage into a smaller, darker, eccentric mass, distinct from karyorrhexis and karyolysis.

questions.title: Peak chromosomal condensation in the cell cycle
questions.question: The highest degree of chromosomal condensation occurs in the following phase of cell cycle:

explanations.A: Correct. Chromosomes reach their most tightly coiled, maximally condensed state at metaphase, when they must line up cleanly at the equatorial plate for the spindle to grip and separate them accurately. This peak condensation is precisely why metaphase chromosomes are the ones photographed and arranged into a karyotype: they are compact and morphologically distinct enough for their banding pattern and centromere position to be read clearly, which is also why colchicine, a drug that blocks spindle formation, is used experimentally to arrest cultured cells in metaphase for karyotyping. By anaphase and telophase the chromosomes are already beginning to decondense again as division completes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Anaphase chromosomes remain condensed as they are pulled apart, but condensation is not increasing further at this stage; the peak has already been reached at metaphase.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Prophase is when chromosomes first become visible as they begin condensing from the interphase chromatin, but condensation is still increasing through prophase, not yet at its maximum.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Interphase chromatin is in its least condensed, most extended state, since this is when the DNA must remain accessible for transcription and replication.
explanations.E: Incorrect. By telophase the chromosomes are decondensing again as the nuclear envelope reforms, moving away from, not toward, peak condensation.

questions.learning_objective: State that chromosomal condensation is greatest at metaphase, which is why metaphase-arrested cells are used for karyotyping.

questions.title: Epithelium lining the thyroid follicle
questions.question: The thyroid follicles are lined by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Simple columnar absorptive epithelium lines an absorptive surface such as the intestine, not the thyroid follicle, which is a secretory, storage-and-release structure rather than an absorptive one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Naming it "secretory" columnar epithelium is close in function but wrong in shape: at the follicle's normal, moderately active state the lining cells are cuboidal, not tall columnar.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Simple squamous epithelium lines the thyroid follicle only in the inactive, colloid-distended state; it is not the follicle's standard, resting description.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Stratified squamous epithelium is a multilayered, protective lining found where friction resistance matters (skin, oesophagus); the thyroid follicle is a single-layered secretory structure, not a protective barrier.
explanations.E: Correct. The thyroid follicle is lined by a single layer of simple cuboidal (cubical) epithelium enclosing a central store of colloid, the site where thyroglobulin is synthesised, iodinated and stored before hormone release. This cuboidal height reflects the follicle's normal, moderately active secretory state; the same follicular cells flatten toward squamous when the gland is under-stimulated and become taller, columnar when strongly stimulated, so cell height itself is a marker of the gland's activity level, but the standard resting description is simple cuboidal.

questions.learning_objective: State that the thyroid follicle is lined by simple cuboidal epithelium at its normal activity state.

questions.title: EM shape of the cell membrane
questions.question: With EM, cell membrane appears ......... in shape:

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Nonolaminar" is not a real membrane-layer description used for the plasma membrane.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Two layers alone would describe only the two leaflets of the phospholipid bilayer without the light space between their tails becoming visible as a distinct middle band; on electron microscopy the membrane resolves into three bands, not two.
explanations.C: Correct. On electron microscopy the plasma membrane is trilaminar — the unit membrane — appearing as two electron-dense (dark) outer layers, corresponding to the polar phospholipid heads and associated protein, separated by one electron-lucent (pale) middle layer, corresponding to the hydrophobic fatty-acid tails. This trilaminar appearance is the basis of the term "unit membrane" and is the standard way every cell membrane, at roughly 7.5 to 10 nm thick, is described on EM regardless of cell type.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Four layers is not the standard EM description of a single plasma membrane; that count would only arise from counting two separate trilaminar membranes side by side, not one.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Five layers is likewise not how a single unit membrane is described on electron microscopy.

questions.learning_objective: State that the plasma membrane appears trilaminar (the unit membrane) on electron microscopy.

questions.title: The double-membranous organelle
questions.question: Which of the following organelles is double membranous?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A lysosome is bounded by a single membrane, not two.
explanations.B: Correct. A mitochondrion is bounded by two membranes: a smooth outer membrane studded with porins, and an inner membrane folded into cristae to expand the surface for oxidative phosphorylation, enclosing a matrix that holds the organelle's own DNA. This two-membrane architecture is unique among the routinely tested cytoplasmic organelles in this list, and it reflects mitochondria's evolutionary origin as engulfed bacteria, each membrane corresponding to a different ancestral boundary.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A ribosome carries no membrane at all; it is a non-membranous organelle built of ribosomal RNA and protein.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The Golgi apparatus is a stack of single-membrane-bound flattened saccules, not a double-membrane structure.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is a network of single-membrane-bound tubules, not double membranous.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the mitochondrion as the double-membrane-bound organelle among the routinely tested cytoplasmic organelles.

questions.title: Organelle responsible for alcohol detoxification
questions.question: Alcohol detoxification is the responsibility of which of the following organelles?

explanations.A: Correct. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum carries the enzymes responsible for detoxifying drugs and toxins, including alcohol, alongside its other cell-type-dependent jobs of lipid and steroid synthesis, and, particularly in muscle as the specialised sarcoplasmic reticulum, regulating intracellular calcium. This detoxifying role is well developed in liver cells, which is why chronic alcohol use drives smooth ER proliferation (hepatocyte hypertrophy) as the liver upregulates this detoxification machinery, and it is a distinct function from the rough ER's protein-export role.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The Golgi apparatus packages and modifies proteins and lipids for secretion or delivery to other compartments; detoxification is not one of its functions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mitochondria generate ATP through oxidative phosphorylation; while alcohol metabolism eventually feeds into mitochondrial pathways, the detoxifying enzymatic step itself belongs to smooth ER, not the mitochondrion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Rough endoplasmic reticulum, marked by its bound ribosomes, synthesises and segregates protein for export; it does not carry the drug-detoxifying enzymes that smooth ER does.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lysosomes digest phagocytosed material and worn-out organelles using acid hydrolases; drug and alcohol detoxification is a distinct, smooth-ER-specific function, not a lysosomal one.

questions.learning_objective: Name smooth endoplasmic reticulum as the organelle responsible for drug and alcohol detoxification.

questions.title: A true statement about the Golgi apparatus on EM
questions.question: Which is true regarding the EM of Golgi apparatus?

options.B: The immature face releases secretory vesicles
options.C: Transfer vesicles are larger than secretory vesicles
options.D: Some secretory vesicles stay as primary lysosomes

explanations.A: Incorrect. It is the immature (cis, entry) face that is typically described as convex, facing the rough endoplasmic reticulum it receives transfer vesicles from; the mature (trans, exit) face is concave.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It is the mature (trans) face, not the immature (cis) face, that buds off the secretory vesicles the Golgi releases; the immature face is where incoming transfer vesicles are received, not where outgoing vesicles are released.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transfer vesicles, which carry material from rough ER to the Golgi's entry face, are smaller than the secretory vesicles budded from the exit face, not larger.
explanations.D: Correct. Not every vesicle budded from the Golgi's mature (trans) face is destined for immediate secretion: some of these vesicles instead remain within the cell as primary lysosomes, membrane-bound sacs of newly packaged hydrolytic enzymes not yet fused with any substrate. This is the same trans-Golgi network that sorts its output into at least two destinies — export via secretory vesicles, or retention as primary lysosomes for the cell's own digestive use — which is why the Golgi is described as central to both the secretory and the lysosomal pathway.
explanations.E: Incorrect. It is the mature (trans) face that is concave, cupping around the forming secretory vesicles; the immature (cis) face is convex.

questions.learning_objective: State that some of the Golgi's trans-face secretory vesicles are retained inside the cell as primary lysosomes rather than being exported.

questions.title: The protein of the mitotic spindle
questions.question: Which of the followings represents the molecular structure of mitotic spindle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Actin is the protein of the microfilament, which cleaves the cell at the end of division (the cleavage furrow); it does not itself build the mitotic spindle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Myosin is the motor protein that partners actin in the thick filament of contraction; it plays no role in spindle formation.
explanations.C: Correct. The mitotic spindle is built of microtubules, which are themselves polymers of alpha- and beta-tubulin dimers arranged into a hollow, 24 nm cylinder of thirteen protofilaments. Microtubules assembled from tubulin radiate from the centrioles at each pole to form the spindle apparatus that captures chromosomes at their kinetochores and pulls the chromatids apart in anaphase; this same tubulin-built spindle is the target of chemotherapy drugs that block microtubule formation to arrest dividing cancer cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Desmin is an intermediate filament protein specific to muscle cells; it is a structural, supportive filament, not the spindle apparatus.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cytokeratin is the intermediate filament protein of epithelial cells; like desmin, it is unrelated to the mitotic spindle.

questions.learning_objective: Name tubulin (microtubules) as the protein that builds the mitotic spindle.

questions.title: When the nuclear membrane dissolves in mitosis
questions.question: In which phase of mitosis the nuclear membrane dissolves?

explanations.A: Correct. During prophase, as the chromosomes condense into visible threads and the nucleoli disappear, the nuclear envelope itself also breaks down, releasing the condensing chromosomes into the general cytoplasm where the forming spindle can reach them. This nuclear envelope breakdown is one of prophase's defining events, alongside chromosome condensation and the start of spindle formation from the microtubule-organising centre, and it is a necessary step before the chromosomes can be captured by spindle microtubules at their kinetochores in metaphase.
explanations.B: Incorrect. By metaphase the nuclear envelope has already dissolved, in prophase; metaphase is instead defined by chromosome alignment at the equatorial plate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Anaphase, the separation of sister chromatids to opposite poles, occurs after the nuclear envelope has already broken down in prophase.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Telophase is when the nuclear envelope re-forms around each set of separated chromosomes, the reverse event, not when it dissolves.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cytokinesis is the physical division of the cytoplasm, occurring after telophase has already re-established two nuclear envelopes; it has nothing to do with the envelope's original dissolution.

questions.learning_objective: State that the nuclear envelope dissolves during prophase of mitosis.

questions.title: The karyotype of Turner's syndrome
questions.question: Suzi, a 20-year old girl attended the outpatient clinic of gynecology, complaining of delayed onset of menstruation. She was referred to do karyotyping which confirmed the diagnosis of Turner's syndrome. Which is the karyotype of this case?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 46,XX is a normal female karyotype, not the monosomic pattern of Turner's syndrome.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 46,XY is a normal male karyotype, unrelated to Turner's syndrome, which affects females.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 47,XXX (triple X syndrome) is a numerical sex-chromosome trisomy, not Turner's syndrome's monosomy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 47,XX+21 is the karyotype of a female with Down syndrome (trisomy 21), an unrelated autosomal abnormality with no sex-chromosome defect.
explanations.E: Correct. Turner's syndrome is monosomy of the X chromosome: the karyotype is 45,XO — 45 total chromosomes, with a single X and no second sex chromosome. This missing sex chromosome underlies the syndrome's underdeveloped genital system and delayed or absent menstruation, exactly Suzi's presentation, and it is the one syndrome in this teaching set that is a chromosome short (45) rather than an extra chromosome (47), which is the classic trap this question sets against Down and Klinefelter syndromes.

questions.learning_objective: State that Turner's syndrome is 45,XO — monosomy of the X chromosome.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.14, دفعة 62 Exams block Q14

questions.title: A structural chromosomal abnormality
questions.question: Which of the followings is a structural chromosomal abnormality?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is a numerical abnormality — an extra whole chromosome — not a structural change to a chromosome's own architecture.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Turner's syndrome (45,XO) is a numerical abnormality — a missing whole chromosome — not a structural one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. YY syndrome (47,XYY) is a numerical abnormality, an extra whole Y chromosome, not a structural rearrangement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Multiple X syndrome (47,XXX) is likewise a numerical abnormality, an extra whole X chromosome.
explanations.E: Correct. Wolf (Wolf-Hirschhorn) syndrome is caused by a structural abnormality — a partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 4 — rather than by a change in the total chromosome count. Structural aberrations alter a chromosome's own architecture through breakage and rejoining (deletion, inversion, translocation, ring formation) while the chromosome number itself may stay normal, in contrast to numerical aberrations such as the trisomies and monosomies listed as the other four options, which change how many whole chromosomes are present without altering any single chromosome's internal structure. Cri-du-chat, a deletion of chromosome 5p, is the more commonly taught partner example of this same structural category.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish a structural chromosomal abnormality (Wolf syndrome, a 4p deletion) from a numerical one (Down, Turner, YY, triple-X).

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.15, دفعة 62 Exams block Q15

questions.title: The mitotic phase karyotyping arrests at
questions.question: In karyotyping, mitosis is arrested in which of the following phases?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Prophase precedes the point of maximal, cleanly separable chromosome condensation; standard karyotyping does not stop cells here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. High-resolution karyotyping specifically arrests cells earlier, at prophase/prometaphase, precisely to resolve smaller structural abnormalities than standard metaphase karyotyping can — but conventional, routine karyotyping is not arrested at this stage.
explanations.C: Correct. Standard karyotyping arrests dividing cells in culture at metaphase using a spindle poison such as colchicine, which inhibits mitotic spindle formation so the chromatids cannot be pulled apart into anaphase. Metaphase is chosen because chromosomal condensation is at its maximum then, giving the sharpest, most distinct chromosome morphology and banding pattern for the cytogeneticist to photograph, sort by size and centromere position, and read for numerical or structural abnormalities. Without this pharmacological arrest, actively dividing cells would proceed past metaphase too quickly to reliably capture and image.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Anaphase chromosomes are already being pulled apart and would give a distorted, unreadable image; karyotyping is arrested before this stage is reached.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Telophase chromosomes have begun decondensing as the nuclear envelope reforms, which would make them unsuitable for the sharp morphology karyotyping needs.

questions.learning_objective: State that karyotyping arrests dividing cells at metaphase, using a spindle-poison such as colchicine, when chromosome condensation is maximal.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.15, دفعة 62 Exams block Q16

questions.title: Site of simple columnar absorptive epithelium
questions.question: Simple columnar absorptive epithelium lines:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The oesophagus is lined by stratified squamous non-keratinised epithelium, suited to resisting the abrasion of a passing food bolus, not to absorption.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The gastric fundus is lined by simple columnar epithelium, but its cells are secretory (mucous-secreting surface cells over the gastric glands), not absorptive.
explanations.C: Correct. The small and large intestine are lined by simple columnar absorptive epithelium, whose surface (enterocytes) cells carry an apical brush border of microvilli that vastly increases the surface area available for absorbing digested nutrients, water and electrolytes. This absorptive columnar lining, interspersed with mucus-secreting goblet cells, is the epithelium's defining functional feature and is what distinguishes the intestine from the stomach's secretory columnar lining or the oesophagus's protective squamous one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pylorus, part of the stomach, is lined by simple columnar epithelium that is secretory (mucous and pyloric gland cells), not absorptive.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The peritoneum is lined by simple squamous epithelium (mesothelium), not columnar absorptive epithelium.

questions.learning_objective: State that simple columnar absorptive epithelium lines the intestine.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.15, دفعة 62 Exams block Q18

questions.title: Where gap junctions are found among the listed tissues
questions.question: Which one of the followings contain gap junction?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Capillary endothelium is joined mainly by tight and adherens-type junctions appropriate to a selective barrier; gap junctions are not its defining lateral junction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Small intestinal epithelium is joined by the junctional complex — zonula occludens, zonula adherens and desmosome — not primarily by gap junctions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Keratinocytes are joined chiefly by desmosomes, which give the epidermis the mechanical strength to resist friction and shear; gap junctions are not their characteristic junction.
explanations.D: Correct. Cardiac muscle fibres are individual cells, each with its own nucleus and membrane, joined end to end at intercalated discs. Those discs carry gap junctions in their lateral portion, low-resistance channels that let an action potential spread rapidly from one myocyte to the next almost as though no membrane separated them, which is what lets cardiac muscle behave as a functional syncytium — the whole atrial mass and the whole ventricular mass each contracting together as a single unit under the all-or-none law, even though the individual cells remain anatomically separate.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Skeletal muscle fibres are formed by fusion of many myoblasts into one true, multinucleated syncytium; they have no intercalated discs and no gap junctions, since a single continuous cell membrane needs no cell-to-cell electrical coupling.

questions.learning_objective: Identify cardiac muscle's intercalated discs, via their gap junctions, as the site of electrical coupling that gives cardiac muscle its functional-syncytium behaviour.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.15, دفعة 62 Exams block Q19

questions.title: The apical surface of taste cells
questions.question: Which one of the followings is a character of taste cells?

options.D: The basal surface shows basal infoldings

explanations.A: Incorrect. True motile cilia, with their 9+2 axoneme, are a feature of respiratory and oviductal epithelium, not of taste cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Stereocilia — long, non-motile microvilli — are the feature of the epididymal epithelium and the inner ear's hair cells, not of taste cells.
explanations.C: Correct. Each taste (gustatory) cell within a taste bud extends short apical microvilli, sometimes called taste hairs, into the taste pore at the epithelial surface, where they carry the receptor sites that first contact tastant molecules dissolved in saliva. This microvillous apical surface maximises the receptive area exposed at the pore, and it is a structural feature the taste cell shares with many other sensory and absorptive cells whose job depends on maximising surface contact rather than on active movement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Basal infoldings that increase basal surface area for active ion transport are a feature of cells such as the striated duct cell or the kidney's proximal tubule cell, not of taste cells.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Desmosomes are a general lateral anchoring junction found in many epithelia under mechanical stress; they are not a defining, specific character of taste cells.

questions.learning_objective: State that the taste cell's apical surface carries microvilli extending into the taste pore.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.15, دفعة 62 Exams block Q20

questions.title: A true statement about cell membrane structure
questions.question: Which one characterizes the structure of cell membrane?

options.A: Cholesterol is less abundant than phospholipids
options.D: Phospholipids are organized in a triple layer

explanations.A: Correct. The cell membrane's lipid component is chiefly a phospholipid bilayer, with cholesterol interspersed among the phospholipid fatty-acid tails in a smaller amount that restricts phospholipid movement and stabilises the membrane. Phospholipids, not cholesterol, are the dominant, most abundant lipid species that build the bilayer's basic framework, with cholesterol present as a modulating, less abundant component rather than an equal or dominant one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It is the phospholipid heads that are hydrophilic (water-loving), facing outward toward the aqueous solution on either side of the membrane; the tails, not the heads, are hydrophobic.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Phospholipids themselves do not form channels; ion and water channels are built from integral (transmembrane) proteins embedded within the lipid bilayer, not from the lipid molecules.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Phospholipids are organised as a bilayer — two layers — not a triple layer; the trilaminar appearance seen on electron microscopy comes from the two dense head-group layers flanking one pale tail-region layer, not from three separate phospholipid layers.
explanations.E: Incorrect. It is the phospholipid heads, not the tails, that are hydrophilic; the tails are hydrophobic and orient inward, away from the surrounding water.

questions.learning_objective: State that cholesterol is present in the cell membrane in a smaller amount than the phospholipids that build its bilayer.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.16, دفعة 62 Exams block Q21

questions.title: Identifying a cell inclusion
questions.question: Which one of the following is a cell inclusion?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Actin is a cytoskeletal protein (the microfilament), classed as a living, essential, non-membranous organelle component, not a non-living inclusion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cytokeratin is an intermediate filament protein, part of the living cytoskeleton, not an inclusion.
explanations.C: Correct. Lipofuscin is an endogenous pigment, classed as a cell inclusion rather than an organelle: cytoplasmic inclusions are non-living, temporary, usually non-essential products of the cell's own activity, in contrast with organelles, which are living, permanent and essential. Lipofuscin specifically is the "age pigment," the undigested residue that accumulates in residual bodies within long-lived, non-dividing cells such as cardiac muscle and neurons as they age, and it sits alongside stored food (glycogen, fat) and other pigments (haemoglobin, melanin, carbon/dust) in this inclusion category.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Myosin is the motor protein of the thick filament, a living, functional cytoskeletal/contractile component, not an inclusion.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Tubulin is the protein of the microtubule, a living, essential cytoskeletal element, not a cell inclusion.

questions.learning_objective: Identify lipofuscin as a cell inclusion (an endogenous pigment), distinct from the living cytoskeletal proteins offered as distractors.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.16, دفعة 62 Exams block Q24

questions.title: Chromosomes carrying a secondary constriction
questions.question: Which one of the following chromosomes has a secondary constriction?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chromosome group 1-3 are large metacentric or submetacentric chromosomes; the secondary constriction/satellite feature belongs to the small acrocentric chromosomes, not this group.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Group 4-6 chromosomes are not the acrocentric, satellite-bearing group carrying a secondary constriction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Group 7-9 chromosomes are likewise not the acrocentric group associated with a secondary constriction and satellites.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Group 10-12 chromosomes are not the acrocentric, satellite-carrying group either.
explanations.E: Correct. Chromosomes 13, 14 and 15 belong to the acrocentric group, whose centromere sits close to one end, leaving a very short arm — and, except on the Y chromosome, some acrocentric chromosomes carry a satellite, a small mass of chromatin attached to that short arm by a narrow secondary constriction containing the ribosomal RNA genes. This D-group (13-15) is one of the two acrocentric, satellite-bearing chromosome groups in the human karyotype, the other being the G-group (21-22), and the secondary constriction/satellite feature is exactly what distinguishes these acrocentric chromosomes from the metacentric and submetacentric groups.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the acrocentric 13-15 chromosome group as carrying a satellite attached by a secondary constriction.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.16, دفعة 62 Exams block Q25

questions.title: The connective tissue type that shows areolae
questions.question: Which type of the connective tissue proper shows areolae?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Elastic connective tissue is dominated by elastic fibres arranged as sheets or lamellae, not open spaces called areolae.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Irregular white fibrous (dense irregular) connective tissue has thick, densely packed collagen bundles running in multiple directions, leaving little open space, unlike loose tissue's areolae.
explanations.C: Correct. Loose (areolar) connective tissue, the commonest connective tissue proper, is identified by both collagen and elastic fibres running loosely through an abundant matrix, with fibroblast nuclei scattered between them and open spaces — the areolae — that hold tissue fluid. These areolae, giving the tissue its alternative name "areolar tissue," are exactly what distinguish it under the microscope from the fibrous connective tissue types, whose fibres are instead condensed into bundles that fill the field with little open space.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mucoid connective tissue (as in Wharton's jelly) is dominated by an abundant, gel-like ground substance with sparse fibres, not by the open areolae of loose connective tissue.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Regular white fibrous (dense regular) connective tissue, as in tendon, has parallel, tightly packed collagen bundles with essentially no open space between them.

questions.learning_objective: Identify loose (areolar) connective tissue as the connective tissue proper that shows areolae.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.17, دفعة 62 Exams block Q27

questions.title: Connective tissue surrounding a single nerve fibre
questions.question: Which one of the following connective tissue surrounds a single nerve fiber?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Endomysium is the fine connective tissue around an individual skeletal muscle fibre, the muscle-tissue analogue of endoneurium, not a nerve covering.
explanations.B: Correct. A peripheral nerve trunk is wrapped, from outside in, by the epineurium around the whole trunk, the perineurium around each individual fascicle, and the endoneurium, a fine connective tissue around each individual nerve fibre within a fascicle. Endoneurium is therefore the innermost, finest of the three coverings, in direct contact with the single nerve fibre and its Schwann cell sheath, distinguishing it from the coarser epineurium and the fascicle-level perineurium.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Epineurium is the outermost, dense connective tissue sheath around the whole nerve trunk, encompassing many fascicles, not a single fibre.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Perimysium surrounds a bundle (fascicle) of muscle fibres, the muscle-tissue analogue of the nerve's perineurium, not a single nerve fibre.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Perineurium surrounds each fascicle (bundle of many nerve fibres) and, through its own tight junctions, forms the blood-nerve barrier; it wraps a bundle of fibres, not a single one.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the endoneurium as the connective tissue layer surrounding a single nerve fibre within a fascicle.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.17, دفعة 62 Exams block Q28

questions.title: The junction that prevents flow between luminal and intercellular fluids
questions.question: Which one of the followings prevents flow of materials between the luminal and intercellular fluids?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A desmosome (macula adherens) is a spot-weld anchoring junction that provides mechanical strength; it does not fuse the intercellular space closed and so does not seal it against fluid flow.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A hemidesmosome anchors a basal cell to the underlying basement membrane, not one cell to its neighbour, so it has no role in sealing the space between adjacent cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Macula adherens is another name for the desmosome; like the desmosome, it anchors without sealing the intercellular space.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The zonula adherens bridges a wide intercellular space with calcium-dependent transmembrane proteins linked to actin filaments; it holds cells together across a real gap rather than closing that gap.
explanations.E: Correct. The zonula occludens, the tight or occluding junction, is where the outer leaflets of two adjacent cell membranes actually fuse at points through transmembrane proteins, leaving no space between them at all, and it encircles the apex of the cell like a belt. This point-fusion is exactly what seals off the paracellular route and prevents material from passing freely between the luminal (surface-facing) and intercellular (basolateral) compartments, forcing anything that crosses the epithelium to go through the cells themselves rather than around them.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the zonula occludens as the junction that fuses adjacent membranes and seals the paracellular space.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.18, دفعة 62 Exams block Q32

questions.title: The organelle without a limiting membrane
questions.question: Which of the following organelles is not covered by a membrane?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is a membranous organelle, a network of membrane-bound tubules and vesicles.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The Golgi apparatus is membranous, a stack of membrane-bound flattened saccules.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mitochondria are membranous — doubly so, bounded by both an outer and an inner membrane.
explanations.D: Correct. Ribosomes, along with the cytoskeleton (and the centrioles, cilia and flagella the microtubules build), are the non-membranous organelles: they have no limiting membrane of their own, unlike the plasma membrane, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes and peroxisomes, which are all bounded by at least one membrane. Ribosomes are instead built directly of ribosomal RNA and protein, free in the cytosol or attached to rough ER, which is exactly why they are classed separately from the membranous organelle group in this basic organelle classification.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lysosomes are membranous, single-membrane-bound sacs of hydrolytic enzymes.

questions.learning_objective: Identify ribosomes as non-membranous, in contrast with the membrane-bound organelles offered as distractors.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.18, دفعة 62 Exams block Q33

questions.title: The diameter of intermediate filaments
questions.question: What is the diameter of intermediate filaments?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 15-18 nm is not the intermediate filament's diameter range; it is closer to a microtubule's 24 nm, though still not matching it either.
explanations.B: Correct. Intermediate filaments are 8-10 nm across, sitting between the thinner microfilament (5-7 nm, built of actin) and the thicker microtubule (24 nm, built of tubulin) in diameter — the middle size that gives this cytoskeletal element its name. They are supportive rather than motile, built from tissue-specific tetrameric protein subunits (cytokeratin in epithelium, desmin in muscle, vimentin in connective tissue, neurofilament protein in neurons, glial fibrillary acidic protein in glia, and lamins in the nuclear envelope), which is why identifying the intermediate filament protein of a tumour by immunocytochemistry can reveal the cell type it arose from.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 6-8 nm sits closer to the microfilament's own 5-7 nm range, not the intermediate filament's 8-10 nm.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 4-6 nm is close to the microfilament's diameter, not the intermediate filament's.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 18-20 nm is too large for the intermediate filament and does not match any of the three main cytoskeletal elements' standard diameters.

questions.learning_objective: State that intermediate filaments are 8-10 nm in diameter, between the microfilament and the microtubule.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.18, دفعة 62 Exams block Q34

questions.title: Identifying an exogenous pigment
questions.question: Which of the followings is an exogenous pigment?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Haemoglobin is an endogenous pigment, produced by the body's own red blood cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Melanin is an endogenous pigment, synthesised by the body's own melanocytes.
explanations.C: Correct. Cell inclusions include pigments, which are classed as either endogenous (made by the body itself — haemoglobin, melanin, lipofuscin) or exogenous (originating outside the body and taken in — carbon and dust, carotene, tattoo dyes). Dust particles, most classically inhaled carbon particles deposited in lung macrophages (as in anthracosis), are the standard example of an exogenous pigment, entering the body from the external environment rather than being synthesised by any of the body's own cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bilirubin, the breakdown product of haem, is an endogenous pigment, produced internally from the body's own haemoglobin catabolism.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lipofuscin is an endogenous pigment, the age-related residual-body pigment produced by the cell's own incomplete digestion of its worn-out material.

questions.learning_objective: Identify dust as an exogenous pigment, distinct from the endogenous pigments offered as distractors.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.18, دفعة 62 Exams block Q35

questions.title: The collagen fibre type present in bone
questions.question: Choose the type of collagen fibers present in the bone:

explanations.A: Correct. Type I collagen forms about 90% of bone's protein content, assembled from two alpha-1 chains and one alpha-2 chain, with type V present in bone only as a minor accessory collagen. This type I collagen framework, mineralised by hydroxyapatite deposited with the help of osteoblast-secreted, vitamin-K-dependent osteocalcin, is what gives bone its combination of tensile flexibility (from the collagen) and rigidity (from the mineral).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Type II collagen forms 90-98% of the total collagen in cartilage, assembled from three identical alpha-1 chains; it is cartilage's, not bone's, principal collagen.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Type III collagen is the reticular fibre type, found in loose connective tissue, lymphoid organs and blood vessel walls, not bone's dominant collagen.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Type IV collagen is the basement membrane collagen, forming the meshwork of the basal lamina, not the dominant fibre type of bone matrix.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Type V collagen is present in bone only as a minor accessory collagen alongside the dominant type I, not as bone's principal collagen type.

questions.learning_objective: State that type I collagen is the predominant collagen of bone.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.19, دفعة 62 Exams block Q38

questions.title: What the horny cell layer of the skin contains
questions.question: The horny cell layer of the skin contains:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hard keratin is the keratin type found in the hair shaft and nail, a denser, sulfur-rich form; the epidermis's own horny layer is built of soft keratin, not hard.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Keratohyaline granules are found in the stratum granulosum, one layer beneath the horny layer, where they contribute the material that helps convert tonofilaments into keratin as the cell moves upward; they are not what the fully cornified horny layer itself contains.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Prekeratin (tonofilament) filaments are the intermediate filament precursor material of the deeper, still-living epidermal layers (basal and prickle cell layers), before full keratinisation, not the final content of the horny layer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Eleidin, a keratohyaline-derived precursor substance, is characteristic of the stratum lucidum, the thin clear layer seen only in thick (non-hairy) skin between the granular and horny layers, not of the horny layer itself.
explanations.E: Correct. The horny layer (stratum corneum) is the fully keratinised, anucleate surface layer of the epidermis, and the keratin that fills its flattened dead cells is soft keratin — pliable and continuously shed and replaced — distinct from the harder, more rigid keratin of hair and nail. This distinction between soft epidermal keratin and hard hair/nail keratin reflects their different jobs: the epidermis needs a flexible, renewable barrier, while hair and nail need a rigid, durable structure.

questions.learning_objective: State that the epidermal horny layer contains soft keratin, distinct from the hard keratin of hair and nail.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.19, دفعة 62 Exams block Q40

questions.title: The organelle that divides to increase its own number
questions.question: Which of the following organelles can divide and increase in number?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rough endoplasmic reticulum has no autonomous, self-templated duplication mechanism of its own; it is built up as membrane and protein are delivered to it, not by dividing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum, like rough ER, is built up from membrane and protein rather than dividing to increase its own numbers.
explanations.C: Correct. Mitochondria divide by fission to increase their own numbers, a self-replicating property they share with centrioles (which duplicate once per cell cycle) but not with the Golgi complex, which has no such autonomous duplication mechanism and is instead built up from membrane and protein delivered to it by the secretory pathway. This capacity for independent division, together with their own mitochondrial DNA, is part of why mitochondria are thought to have originated as once free-living, engulfed bacteria.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The Golgi apparatus has no autonomous duplication mechanism; it is assembled from membrane and protein trafficked to it, not by dividing itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lysosomes are formed by budding from the Golgi's trans face, packaged from enzymes made on the rough ER; they do not divide to increase their own number.

questions.learning_objective: State that mitochondria divide by fission to increase their own numbers, unlike the Golgi apparatus.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.20, دفعة 61 Exams block Q1

questions.title: Which ribosomes make protein the cell keeps
questions.question: Which of the following synthesis protein used within the cell?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Attached (rough-ER-bound) ribosomes synthesise protein destined for export, insertion into membranes, or the lysosomal/secretory pathway, not protein the cell simply keeps for its own cytosolic use.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rough endoplasmic reticulum, studded with attached ribosomes, is likewise dedicated to synthesising exported or membrane-bound protein, not the cell's own retained protein.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages protein already synthesised elsewhere; it does not itself synthesise protein for either internal use or export.
explanations.D: Correct. Free ribosomes, scattered singly or in rosette clusters through the cytosol rather than bound to membrane, synthesise protein that the cell retains and uses for itself — structural and enzymatic proteins that stay in the cytoplasm — as opposed to attached (rough-ER-bound) ribosomes, which make protein destined for export or for insertion into membranes. Both free and attached ribosomes contribute to a cell's overall basophilia, since it is the phosphate-rich ribosomal RNA in either location that binds haematoxylin, but only the free population's product stays within the cell that made it.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum carries no ribosomes at all and has no role in protein synthesis; its jobs are lipid/steroid synthesis, detoxification and, in muscle, calcium regulation.

questions.learning_objective: State that free ribosomes synthesise protein retained for the cell's own use, as distinct from attached-ribosome/rER protein made for export.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.20, دفعة 61 Exams block Q2

questions.title: What euchromatin represents
questions.question: Euchromatin:

options.C: Represents the coiled parts of chromosomal threads

explanations.A: Incorrect. It is heterochromatin, the tightly packed form, whose DNA is inaccessible and therefore transcriptionally inactive; euchromatin is the form that does direct protein synthesis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Nuclear pores are a feature of the nuclear envelope itself, not a property that distinguishes euchromatin from heterochromatin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Coiled, condensed chromosomal threads describe heterochromatin, not euchromatin, which is the loosely extended, uncoiled form.
explanations.D: Correct. Euchromatin is the loosely extended, decondensed form of chromatin, in contrast with the tightly coiled heterochromatin. Because its DNA is open and accessible to the transcription machinery, euchromatin is the transcriptionally active form that carries the genes actually being expressed, while heterochromatin's dense packing keeps its DNA silenced. This same loose packing means euchromatin does not stain as a distinct dark clump on light microscopy the way heterochromatin does; instead it simply contributes to the pale, finely stippled background of the nucleoplasm.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Basophilic, darkly staining chromatin granules describe heterochromatin's light-microscopic appearance; euchromatin is comparatively pale and not resolved as a distinct clump.

questions.learning_objective: State that euchromatin is the extended, transcriptionally active form of chromatin that carries active genes.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer-letter column, render p.20, دفعة 61 Exams block Q3

questions.title: Epithelium lining the upper respiratory tract
questions.question: Which of the following lines the upper respiratory tract?

options.D: Pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with goblet cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. Simple squamous epithelium lines sites built for rapid diffusion, such as the alveolus, not the mucus-and-cilia-dependent conducting airway.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Stratified columnar epithelium is an uncommon epithelial type found at a few transition zones (such as parts of the conjunctiva or male urethra), not the standard lining of the respiratory conducting portion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Simple columnar epithelium alone, without the pseudostratified, ciliated, goblet-cell-bearing features, is the intestinal absorptive/secretory type, not the respiratory conducting epithelium.
explanations.D: Correct. Most of the conducting portion of the respiratory system — including the nasal cavity, most of which is lined by this same epithelium — is lined by pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with goblet cells. Its ciliated columnar cells (the most numerous type) beat mucus, with its trapped bacteria and dust, outward toward the pharynx, its mucous goblet cells secrete that mucus, and its basal cells serve as the stem-cell population that replaces the other cell types, together forming the mucociliary escalator that clears the airway.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Transitional epithelium (urothelium) lines the urinary tract, not the respiratory tract.

questions.learning_objective: State that the upper respiratory tract is lined by pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with goblet cells.

questions.title: The connective tissue cell that may be fixed or free
questions.question: Which of the following cells might be fixed or free in connective tissue?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The fibroblast is always a fixed, resident connective tissue cell; it does not circulate or wander as a free cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The mast cell is a free connective tissue cell throughout, not one that is sometimes fixed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The plasma cell is a free, typically short-lived connective tissue cell, not one with a fixed, resident form.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The adipose (fat) cell is a fixed, resident connective tissue cell; it does not exist in a free, wandering form.
explanations.E: Correct. The macrophage exists in two states: as a fixed, resident histiocyte sitting quietly in the connective tissue of a given organ, and as a free, actively wandering, phagocytic cell that migrates to a site of injury or infection in response to chemotactic signals. This dual capacity — the same monocyte-derived lineage able to sit resident or actively patrol — sets it apart from cells such as the fibroblast and adipose cell, which are always fixed, and the mast cell and plasma cell, which are always free.

questions.learning_objective: State that the macrophage exists as both a fixed (histiocyte) and a free (wandering) connective tissue cell.

A reused Kasr concept (CON-FND-7D55448AC644C5) instead sorts the same five cell types into a strict fixed/free binary that places the macrophage only under "free" alongside the mast and plasma cells — a different classroom framing of the same cell list. Both are standard teaching traditions; the printed key of this Mansoura source stands, and the discrepancy is logged here rather than silently resolved.

questions.title: The connective tissue cell that secretes SRS-A
questions.question: Which of the following CT cell is responsible for secretion of slow reacting substance of anaphylaxis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The fibroblast synthesises the connective tissue's fibres and ground substance; it has no role in the mediators of an allergic reaction.
explanations.B: Correct. The mast cell's granules store heparin and histamine and, on IgE-triggered degranulation, also release eosinophil chemotactic factor and leukotrienes — the leukotriene mixture classically termed the slow reacting substance of anaphylaxis (SRS-A), so called because its bronchoconstrictor and vascular effects develop more slowly than histamine's immediate action but last longer. This IgE-triggered release is the mast cell's central role in the immediate allergic reaction, producing locally itching, swelling and wheal, and systemically the vasodilation, increased permeability, bronchospasm and pressure drop of anaphylactic shock.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The plasma cell manufactures and secretes antibody; it does not store or release SRS-A/leukotrienes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The adipose cell stores triglyceride for energy; it has no role in anaphylactic mediator release.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The macrophage phagocytoses and presents antigen; SRS-A/leukotriene release in the immediate allergic reaction is a mast-cell function, not a macrophage one.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the mast cell as the connective tissue cell that releases the leukotriene mixture known as SRS-A.

questions.title: A true statement about ependymal cells
questions.question: Which of the followings is true regarding ependymal cells?

options.C: Line ventricles of brain & spinal cord

explanations.A: Incorrect. Phagocytosis is microglia's job, not the ependymal cell's; ependymal cells are epithelial-like lining cells, not resident immune phagocytes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Myelinating CNS axons is the oligodendrocyte's function, not the ependymal cell's.
explanations.C: Correct. Ependymal cells are the ciliated or cuboidal, epithelial-like cells that line the cavities containing cerebrospinal fluid — the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord — and contribute to CSF circulation, with a specialised, secretory subset forming the choroid plexus epithelium that helps produce CSF. This lining function, distinct from the other glial cell types' roles (support, myelination, phagocytosis), is the ependymal cell's defining feature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Myelinating PNS axons is the Schwann cell's function, not the ependymal cell's.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Metabolically supporting neurons is chiefly the astrocyte's function, through its end-feet on capillaries and its role in the blood-brain barrier, not the ependymal cell's.

questions.learning_objective: State that ependymal cells line the CSF-containing ventricles and central canal.

questions.title: A feature of thick skin
questions.question: Thick skin has:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Thick (non-hairy) skin, confined to the palms and soles, lacks hair follicles altogether; hair follicles are a feature of thin (hairy) skin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Thick skin also lacks sebaceous glands, since these develop as outgrowths of the hair follicle and thick skin has no follicles for them to arise from.
explanations.C: Incorrect. It is thin skin, not thick skin, that carries comparatively fewer sweat glands; thick skin, at the palms and soles, is in fact rich in eccrine sweat glands.
explanations.D: Correct. Thick skin's thick, ridged epidermis interdigitates with numerous, tall dermal papillae, and this ridged surface pattern is exactly what produces fingerprints — the friction ridges of the palms and soles used for grip and, forensically, for identification. Thick skin is confined to the palms, soles and the tips and sides of the fingers and toes, has a much thicker epidermis (400-1400 micrometres) than thin skin, and lacks hair follicles, sebaceous glands and arrector pili muscles altogether, while carrying abundant sweat glands.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Thick skin lacks arrector pili muscles, since these attach to hair follicles and thick skin has none; arrector pili muscles are a feature of thin (hairy) skin.

questions.learning_objective: State that thick skin's ridged dermal papillae produce fingerprints, and that thick skin lacks hair follicles, sebaceous glands and arrector pili.

questions.title: Where hair colour pigment sits
questions.question: The color of the hair is due to pigments which are present in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The hair medulla is the hair's thin, often discontinuous central core; it is not the site where the pigment responsible for hair colour is concentrated.
explanations.B: Correct. The hair cortex, the thick middle layer of the hair shaft that makes up the bulk of its substance and contains the keratin-filled spindle-shaped cortical cells, is where melanin granules (transferred into the growing hair from matrix melanocytes) are deposited, and it is this pigment within the cortex that gives the hair its colour. The cortex's dense keratin filaments also give the hair shaft most of its strength and flexibility, so the same layer both determines colour and provides the hair's principal mechanical substance.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The hair cuticle is the thin, single-layered, overlapping outer scale layer of the shaft; it protects the cortex but is not where colour pigment accumulates.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The outer root sheath is a layer of the hair follicle itself, continuous with the epidermis, not a pigment-bearing layer of the hair shaft.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The connective tissue sheath surrounds the outside of the follicle; it plays no role in the hair shaft's own pigmentation.

questions.learning_objective: State that hair colour pigment is deposited in the hair cortex.

questions.title: A true statement about the Golgi apparatus
questions.question: How would you describe Golgi apparatus?

options.A: Surrounds the nucleus of epithelial secretory cells
options.C: Could be seen with iron Hx

explanations.A: Incorrect. The Golgi apparatus is sited apically in secretory epithelial cells, or perinuclearly in nerve cells; it does not surround the nucleus in epithelial secretory cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lipid and steroid metabolism is smooth endoplasmic reticulum's job, not the Golgi apparatus's; the Golgi's role is packaging and modifying protein and lipid for secretion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Iron haematoxylin is not the classic stain used to demonstrate the Golgi apparatus; silver impregnation is.
explanations.D: Correct. Because the Golgi apparatus is not stained by routine haematoxylin and eosin — showing only as a pale, unstained "negative Golgi image" beside the nucleus — silver impregnation is the classic technique used to demonstrate it, colouring it as a network of brown granules and fibrils. This silver-stained appearance, together with the negative image seen on H&E, are the two standard light-microscopic ways of recognising the Golgi apparatus before ever reaching electron microscopy, where it appears as a stack of three to ten curved saccules.
explanations.E: Incorrect. It is the cis face that is immature (the entry face receiving transfer vesicles from the rough ER); the mature face is the trans (exit) face, not the cis face.

questions.learning_objective: State that the Golgi apparatus, invisible on H&E, is demonstrated by silver impregnation.

questions.title: The site of flagella in the human body
questions.question: Which of the followings is a site of flagella?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The oesophagus is lined by stratified squamous epithelium, which carries no cilia or flagella at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The Fallopian tube is lined in part by ciliated cells whose motile cilia help move the oocyte toward the uterus — true cilia, present in numbers over the cell surface, not a single flagellum.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The small intestine's absorptive epithelium carries microvilli, not cilia or a flagellum.
explanations.D: Correct. The sperm tail is the human body's own flagellum — a single, long motile process built on the same 9+2 microtubule axoneme as a cilium, but present singly per cell rather than in the numerous short processes typical of ciliated epithelium, and specialised for propelling the whole cell forward rather than for moving fluid or particles over a stationary epithelial surface. This single-process, whole-cell-propelling arrangement is what distinguishes a flagellum from the many shorter cilia of a ciliated epithelial cell, even though both share the same internal axoneme structure.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The ureter is lined by transitional epithelium, which carries neither cilia nor a flagellum.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the sperm tail as the human body's flagellum, distinguishing a single motile flagellum from a ciliated epithelium's many cilia.

questions.title: Cell layers of the full urinary bladder
questions.question: What is the number of cell layers in full urinary bladder?

explanations.A: Correct. As the urinary bladder distends and fills, its transitional epithelium (urothelium) thins and its polyhedral intermediate cells are pushed laterally so the layer count falls to its lowest, per this exam's printed key: 2. The superficial dome-shaped cells flatten out over the stretched surface at this point, which is exactly the distensibility this epithelium is built for — thinning under stretch and thickening again once the bladder empties, all without losing the continuous, urine-impermeable barrier its plaque-covered superficial cells provide.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Four is not the layer count this source's printed key gives for the full bladder.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Eight sits closer to the empty-bladder end of the reported layer-count range, not the full-bladder count this source keys.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ten exceeds the typical range reported for either the empty or the full transitional epithelium.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Twenty is far above any reported layer count for transitional epithelium at any distension state.

questions.learning_objective: State that transitional epithelium thins to its lowest layer count as the urinary bladder distends fully, per this source's printed key.

questions.title: The function of the nucleolus
questions.question: What is the function of nucleolus?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bile acid metabolism is a liver-cell biochemical function unrelated to any nuclear organelle; it is not a nucleolar job.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Exchange between nucleus and cytoplasm is carried out through the nuclear pore complexes of the nuclear envelope, not by the nucleolus itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lipid metabolism is a smooth endoplasmic reticulum function; the nucleolus plays no role in it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. General secretory function belongs to the Golgi apparatus and the secretory pathway, not to the nucleolus.
explanations.E: Correct. The nucleolus is a rounded, deeply basophilic, unbounded mass inside the nucleus whose function is to synthesise ribosomal RNA and assemble ribosomal subunits, which then pass out through the nuclear pores to the cytoplasm to build ribosomes. Its three ultrastructural dark components trace this production line directly — the pars amorpha (the rDNA genes themselves), the pars fibrosa (newly synthesised rRNA) and the pars granulosa (maturing ribosomal subunits) — and a cell's nucleolar size scales with how much protein it is making, which is why large, prominent nucleoli are a feature of both normal protein-secreting cells and rapidly growing malignant ones.

questions.learning_objective: State that the nucleolus's function is to synthesise ribosomal RNA and assemble ribosomal subunits.

questions.title: The connective tissue cell with a chart-wheel nucleus
questions.question: Which of the following connective tissue cells has Chart-Wheel nucleus?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The adipose cell's nucleus is flattened and pushed to the cell's periphery by its single large fat droplet, not cartwheel-shaped.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The fibroblast has an oval or spindle-shaped, pale-staining, open (euchromatic) nucleus appropriate to its high protein-synthetic activity, not a cartwheel pattern.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The macrophage has a kidney-shaped or oval nucleus, not the cartwheel pattern.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The mast cell has a central, spherical, pale nucleus, distinct from the plasma cell's eccentric cartwheel nucleus even though both cells are basophilic and can otherwise be confused.
explanations.E: Correct. The plasma cell is identified by its cartwheel (clock-face) nucleus — heterochromatin clumped radially around the nuclear periphery like the spokes of a wheel — set eccentrically to one side of the cell, beside a pale-staining area corresponding to its well-developed Golgi apparatus. This nuclear pattern, reflecting the cell's intense, sustained antibody-manufacturing activity, is one of the standard cell-identification landmarks taught alongside the neutrophil's multilobed nucleus and the small lymphocyte's dense round one.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the plasma cell by its eccentric cartwheel nucleus beside a pale Golgi area.
